opus-5.5.text:
I find it very promising, and I'd say it's one of the most exciting directions right now, with some important caveats.

The basic insight is that these models have absorbed an enormous amount of human knowledge, including a lot of implicit knowledge about what counts as good, interesting, or correct. So when you put an LLM in a loop where it generates something, evaluates it, and uses that feedback to generate the next thing, you're starting to build systems that can improve without a human in every step. That's very close to what I care about in open-endedness research: systems that keep producing novel and increasingly capable artifacts on their own.

We've explored versions of this ourselves, for example evolving prompts where the model mutates its own prompts and the mutation strategies themselves, or using models to search for adversarial inputs that expose weaknesses in other models. In those settings, the loop really does find things a human wouldn't have thought to try.

But the big caveat is the evaluator. If the model judges its own output, you can get self-reinforcing errors. The generator learns to exploit blind spots in the judge, and you end up optimizing for something that looks good to the model rather than something actually good. That's Goodhart's law. The loop is only as strong as its grounding signal.

So where this works best is where you can anchor the loop in something external and hard to fool: code you can execute, unit tests, a simulator, a game environment, a formal verifier. Then the LLM can be creative on the generation side while the environment keeps it honest. Where you only have the model's own judgment, I'm more cautious. It can still help, especially for notions of interestingness or diversity, but you need to watch for drift and reward hacking.

So: very promising, possibly a key ingredient for open-ended self-improvement. But the real research question is how you design the evaluation so the loop keeps making genuine progress instead of fooling itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes explored self-evaluation loops and says they have found things a human would not have thought to try, communicating demonstrated practical success.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting directions right now, but I'd want to be careful about what exactly the loop is doing, because the devil is in the details.

So the basic idea is very appealing. You have a model that can generate candidate solutions, and you have the same model, or a copy of it, acting as a critic, scoring those outputs, and then you feed that signal back, either in context or through some kind of training. And at a high level that looks like you've closed the loop, you've got something that can improve itself without a human in the loop at every step. That's what got me excited about open-endedness in the first place, this question of whether you can build systems that keep generating their own learning signal indefinitely.

But there's a catch, and it's a fundamental one. If the generator and the evaluator share the same blind spots, the loop doesn't actually give you anything new. The model will happily rate its own hallucinations as excellent. We've seen this in our own experiments. You can get the model to say "yes, this is correct" with great confidence, and it's just wrong, and the critic has the same gap in knowledge as the generator. So self-evaluation alone is kind of a closed system. Information-theoretically, where is the new signal coming from?

Where it does work well, in my view, is when the evaluation is grounded in something outside the model. Code is the obvious example. If the model writes a program and then executes it, and the tests pass or they don't, that's a real signal. It doesn't rely on the model's self-assessment. Math with a formal verifier, same thing. Games where you have a win condition. In those settings, putting an LLM in a loop is extremely powerful, because the model is good at generating diverse candidates and the environment is good at being an honest judge.

And then there's a middle ground that I find really interesting, which is where the model isn't evaluating correctness directly but is evaluating something like interestingness or novelty. That's the sort of thing we looked at with work on open-ended environment generation, where the model proposes new tasks or new environments, and the question is not "is this right" but "is this a useful next thing to learn from." There the model's judgment is actually quite good, because it's drawing on this enormous prior about what humans find interesting. It's a different kind of loop, less about verifying answers and more about steering the search.

So my honest answer is: very promising, provided there's some asymmetry between generating and verifying. Verification being easier than generation is what makes the whole thing work. Where that asymmetry exists, I think these loops could go a long way. Where it doesn't, you're mostly just amplifying the model's existing biases, and you have to be a bit skeptical of the results.

r001.rationale: The response calls grounded loops promising and powerful, but describes code execution and verification conditionally. Its explicit reference to experiments reports failures of self-evaluation, not empirical success.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very promising, particularly in settings where you can get feedback that is grounded in something outside the language model itself. If you’re generating code, for example, you can run it, see whether it passes tests, and use those results to improve the next attempt. That gives you a loop where the model can actually discover that something didn’t work.

The harder case is when you’re asking the model to judge its own answer without any additional evidence. It may catch mistakes, but it can also have the same blind spots as when it produced the answer. So I wouldn’t assume that repeatedly asking, “Are you sure?” necessarily gets you closer to the truth.

What excites me is combining that ability to propose and revise with interaction with an environment. Then you have a system that can try things, observe the consequences, and adapt. The quality of that feedback is really crucial.

r001.rationale: The response calls the approach promising and gives code testing as an example, but does not state that such loops have already demonstrated empirical success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very promising, but a lot depends on what you mean by “evaluate.” If you’re just asking the model to look at its own answer and say whether it’s correct, it can make the same mistake again. Being able to generate a convincing critique doesn’t necessarily mean you can distinguish a correct answer from an incorrect one.

What I find particularly exciting is when that loop is grounded in something external. If the model writes code, it can execute it and look at test results. If it takes an action in an environment, it can observe what happened. Then it has feedback that can actually challenge its assumptions, and it can use that feedback to try something different.

So I think there’s a lot of potential in giving these systems more opportunity to act, get feedback, and revise. The key question is whether the feedback provides new information, rather than simply reinforcing what the model already believes.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the approach as promising and gives examples of external feedback, but does not state that self-evaluation loops have already demonstrated empirical success.
